body.text: [Service providers] can't just have one approach ... they're unable to understand people with a bit more different situation. And then the suggestions that they come up with and the advice, it's like, you’re totally not getting the point, you're not understanding. I've clearly seen that they've dealt with a particular type of women and I'm like ‘I can see where she's coming from’ and I'm like ‘mine's a whole different case’. What [other women have] experienced is not what it is for me. For me it's … having to be really considerate, not to be doing tick boxes at all.
body.source: (Experts by experience discussions, multiple types of accommodation, Asian or Asian British)

body.h2: 7. Looking back on survivors’ journeys and towards solutions
7. Looking back on survivors’ journeys and towards solutions
body.text: While the decision to access accommodation support and services was universally recognised by participants to have been the right decision, not all participants looked back positively on their experiences in accommodations, particularly those in hotels, bed and breakfast accommodation and hostels. It was important for accommodation to be fit for purpose and have appropriate facilities to accommodate day-to-day living.

body.h2: 7. Looking back on survivors’ journeys and towards solutions
body.text: I felt like it was a privilege for me to be in somewhere like that, but I look at it now and I think … I should never have been grateful to be somewhere like that. (Multiple types of accommodation, Mixed or Multiple ethnic group)

body.h2: 7. Looking back on survivors’ journeys and towards solutions
body.text: I felt like it was a privilege for me to be in somewhere like that, but I look at it now and I think … I should never have been grateful to be somewhere like that.
body.source: (Multiple types of accommodation, Mixed or Multiple ethnic group)

body.h2: 7. Looking back on survivors’ journeys and towards solutions
body.text: Among those who felt they had received empathetic support, survivors described such support as making a big difference to their experiences and to their domestic abuse recovery. Participants suggested that more mental health support was needed to help survivors deal with the ongoing impacts of domestic abuse.

body.h2: 7. Looking back on survivors’ journeys and towards solutions
body.text: As much as women have help, particularly speaking for myself, you have the support, you have your key worker that comes to see you every week, but one side that I thought was not looked … into is people’s mental health … accessing even mental help was very difficult … Because I felt suicidal a lot. But my key worker was very good, she was really brilliant. She made loads and loads of referrals. (Refuge, Black African)

body.h2: 7. Looking back on survivors’ journeys and towards solutions
body.text: As much as women have help, particularly speaking for myself, you have the support, you have your key worker that comes to see you every week, but one side that I thought was not looked … into is people’s mental health … accessing even mental help was very difficult … Because I felt suicidal a lot. But my key worker was very good, she was really brilliant. She made loads and loads of referrals.

body.h2: 7. Looking back on survivors’ journeys and towards solutions
body.text: After leaving an abusive situation, survivors saw their lives improving and had the space to build personal strength and confidence. They offered thanks to those who supported them along the way. There was appreciation of both the services they had received during their accommodation journeys and of the staff who provided support to regain their confidence and begin their journey to recovery.

body.h2: 7. Looking back on survivors’ journeys and towards solutions
body.text: I lost my life; I didn’t have a life but [domestic abuse organisation] gave me another life. It let me to live again. Now [domestic abuse organisation] is my second family, the family that caused me to continue living. It gave me another life. (Translated interview, hostel, Other ethnic group)

body.h2: 7. Looking back on survivors’ journeys and towards solutions
body.text: I lost my life; I didn’t have a life but [domestic abuse organisation] gave me another life. It let me to live again. Now [domestic abuse organisation] is my second family, the family that caused me to continue living. It gave me another life.

body.h2: 7. Looking back on survivors’ journeys and towards solutions
body.text: Survivors’ positive reflections of their accommodation journeys and any feelings of gratitude towards support workers and other service providers do not diminish the difficulties they experienced throughout. Nonetheless, participants generally had positive messages for others who may be in similar situations, encouraging them to access accommodation as a first step to ending the domestic abuse and starting their recovery.

body.h2: 9. Glossary
body.h3: Domestic abuse
body.text: Domestic abuse is not limited to physical violence and can include a range of abusive behaviours. It can also be experienced as repeated patterns of abusive behaviour to maintain power and control in a relationship.

body.h2: 9. Glossary
body.h3: Domestic abuse
body.text: The [Domestic Abuse Act 2021](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2021/17/contents/enacted) defines domestic abuse as any incident or pattern of incidents between those aged 16 years and over who:

body.text: are a relative

body.h2: 9. Glossary
body.h3: Domestic abuse
body.text: have, or there has been a time when they each have had, a parental relationship in relation to the same child

body.h2: 9. Glossary
body.h3: Domestic abuse
body.text: The Act recognises children aged under 18 years who see, or hear, or experience the effects of the abuse, as a victim of domestic abuse if they are related or have a parental relationship to the adult victim or perpetrator of the abuse.

body.h2: 9. Glossary

body.h2: 9. Glossary
body.h3: Move-on accommodation and the bidding system
body.text: Move-on accommodation refers to the permanent or longer-term accommodation that survivors access after leaving domestic abuse. This includes council properties, housing association properties, or private rental properties. Council and housing association refer to properties that are secured through the housing register.

body.h2: 9. Glossary
body.h3: Move-on accommodation and the bidding system
body.text: According to [Shelter's housing advice web page](https://england.shelter.org.uk/housing_advice/council_housing_association/how_to_apply_for_council_housing/bidding_and_offers), policies vary across councils, and in some areas, homes are directly offered. The term "bidding system" describes a choice-based scheme in other areas where people who meet the criteria for the properties on the list express their interest in a home, usually online. The council then offer the property to the person on the housing register with the most priority, usually decided based on points or banding.

body.h3: No recourse to public funds
body.text: No recourse to public funds

body.h2: 9. Glossary
body.h3: No recourse to public funds
body.text: The [House of Commons Library](https://commonslibrary.parliament.uk/research-briefings/cbp-9790/#:~:text=Migrants%20in%20the%20UK%20on,%27%2C%20or%20%27NRPF%27.) notes that migrants in the UK on visas, illegally or seeking asylum are usually ineligible for most social welfare benefits and public housing. This is referred to as having "no recourse to public funds" or "NRPF". Most temporary migrants have no recourse to public funds, with human rights exceptions.

body.h2: 9. Glossary
body.h3: No recourse to public funds
body.text: Under the Immigration and Asylum Act 1999, people who do not have any immigration permission, or whose visa comes with an individual NRPF condition, are excluded from benefits and housing. An NRPF condition is mandatory for most types of visas. [Citizens Advice's No Recourse to Public Funds web page](https://www.citizensadvice.org.uk/about-us/our-work/our-campaigns/policy-campaigns/no-recourse-to-public-funds/) notes that this condition excludes eligibility to vital benefits like Universal Credit and Child Benefit, as well as a range of other support like homelessness assistance or access to refuges that rely on public funds to operate.

body.h2: 9. Glossary
body.h3: No recourse to public funds
body.text: A few categories of people, including those granted permission to remain in the UK for human rights reasons, can apply for a "change of conditions" granting them recourse to public funds.

body.h2: 9. Glossary
body.h3: No recourse to public funds
body.text: The list of public funds covers a wide range of social security benefits, tax credits and housing assistance. Local authorities have some statutory duties to support people with NRPF, in particular families with children.

body.h2: 9. Glossary
body.h3: No recourse to public funds
body.text: While making a claim for indefinite leave to remain, people who have come to the UK on a spousal visa are entitled to access accommodation and benefits through the Domestic Violence Destitution Concession for three months.

body.h2: 9. Glossary
body.h3: Accommodation
body.text: This article uses a broad definition of accommodation that recognises the diversity of housing that domestic abuse survivors and their children may live in after leaving domestic abuse. Our research captures the experiences of those in accommodation provided by local authorities or services, such as specialist domestic abuse charities. It does not include privately-provided accommodation. The accommodation referred to includes:

body.h2: 9. Glossary
body.h3: Accommodation
body.text: refuge accommodation, including specialist "by and for" refuges provided by charitable organisations, and local authority-provided refuges

body.h2: 9. Glossary
body.h3: Accommodation
body.text: hotels and bed and breakfasts (B&B), primarily used as emergency accommodation

body.h2: 9. Glossary
body.h3: Accommodation
body.text: hostels, including single-sex, mixed-sex, and mixed-needs hostels

body.h2: 9. Glossary

body.text: self-contained temporary accommodation, mostly provided by local authorities

body.h2: 9. Glossary
body.h3: Accommodation
body.text: shared housing, provided by local authorities

body.h2: 9. Glossary
body.h3: Accommodation
body.text: This is not an exhaustive list of all accommodation types available to survivors. These are the accommodation types that were reported by participants in our research.

body.h2: 9. Glossary
body.h3: Accommodation
body.text: Local housing authorities have duties to prevent and relieve homelessness under Part 7 of the Housing Act 1996. This includes duties to secure accommodation for people with a priority need. This extends priority need for homelessness assistance to eligible people who are homeless because they are a victim of domestic abuse. These changes mean that local authorities have a duty to secure suitable accommodation for eligible people, and any people who normally reside with them, who are homeless because of domestic abuse.

body.h2: 9. Glossary
body.h3: Accommodation
body.text: The Domestic Abuse Act 2021 also places a statutory duty on Tier One local authorities to assess needs across their area and commission adequate support for domestic abuse survivors and their children in identified "safe accommodation". This is defined in statutory guidance on [Domestic abuse support within safe accommodation](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/domestic-abuse-support-within-safe-accommodation). "Safe accommodation" is defined as single-sex, secure, and dedicated to supporting victims of domestic abuse, such as refuge accommodation.

body.h2: 9. Glossary
body.h3: Accommodation
body.text: The Domestic Abuse Act 2021 identifies specific accommodation settings as safe. These include:

body.h2: 9. Glossary
body.h3: Accommodation
body.text: refuge accommodation

body.h2: 9. Glossary
body.h3: Accommodation
body.text: specialist safe accommodation

body.h2: 9. Glossary
body.h3: Accommodation
body.text: dispersed accommodation

body.h2: 9. Glossary
body.h3: Accommodation
body.text: second stage accommodation

body.h2: 9. Glossary
body.h3: Accommodation
body.text: and other forms of domestic abuse emergency accommodation

body.h2: 9. Glossary
body.h3: Accommodation
body.text: In the context of emergency and temporary accommodation, most support focuses on physical safety. However, some researchers suggest it is important to consider "more-than-safety", as described in Bowstead's [Spaces of safety and more-than-safety in women's refuges in England article (PDF, 634KB)](https://pure.royalholloway.ac.uk/ws/portalfiles/portal/30944494/Spaces_of_safety_GPC_2018_AAM_Bowstead.pdf). The concept of more-than-safety suggests that survivors' recovery, autonomy, freedom, and preparation for independence beyond temporary accommodation settings are integral to their safety and protection from harm.

body.h2: 9. Glossary
body.h3: Accommodation
body.text: Refuge

body.h2: 9. Glossary
body.h3: Accommodation
body.text: The term "refuge" was most often used to describe single-sex accommodation provided specifically for survivors of domestic abuse. This accommodation often featured services, such as counselling, workshops and activities for survivors to participate in, and was mostly provided by specialist charities. However, some refuges were provided by the local authority.

body.h2: 9. Glossary
body.h3: Accommodation
body.text: The refuges described most often had individual bedrooms with shared communal spaces, such as kitchens and living room areas, while others were self-contained with their own kitchen and bathroom. The refuges ranged from housing a small number of single survivors to multiple families across 20 flats.

body.h2: 9. Glossary
body.h3: Accommodation
body.text: [🠕 Back to the top of the Glossary](#9-glossary)

body.h2: 9. Glossary
body.h3: Accommodation
body.text: Hotel

body.h2: 9. Glossary
body.h3: Accommodation
body.text: Hotels were a form of "emergency accommodation" that were generally said to consist of an en-suite room in a large building. Some hotels were also open to members of the public. Survivors who stayed in hotels were sometimes caring for young children and described not having access to cooking facilities other than a kettle.

body.h2: 9. Glossary
body.h3: Accommodation
body.text: Hostel

body.h2: 9. Glossary
body.h3: Accommodation
body.text: Hostels, which were sometimes considered to be "emergency accommodation", were mostly described as "mixed-need", meaning they were also used to house other "at-risk" groups, such as those with a history of homelessness or substance misuse. Hostels were often described as requiring residents to share a kitchen and sometimes a bathroom, but were sometimes self-contained except for a laundry room.

body.h2: 9. Glossary
body.h3: Accommodation
body.h4: Shared and self-contained local authority-provided accommodation
body.text: Shared and self-contained local authority-provided accommodation

body.h2: 9. Glossary
body.h3: Accommodation
body.h4: Shared and self-contained local authority-provided accommodation
body.text: Local authority-provided properties varied between self-contained and shared housing. Self-contained accommodations were generally described as flats or studios in mixed-need buildings but did not require residents to share facilities. Shared housing was described as a room within a mixed-need shared house where facilities such as bathrooms, kitchens, living areas and washing facilities were all shared.

body.h2: 9. Glossary
body.h3: Trauma-informed practice
body.text: Trauma-informed practice recognises that individuals' responses are a way of adapting and coping with symptoms of trauma. It requires understanding of the effects of trauma, recognising trauma triggers and trauma responses, and integrating trauma-informed practice into professional conduct or a programme of work, or both.

body.h2: 9. Glossary
body.h3: Trauma-informed practice
body.text: Trauma-informed practice is based upon strengths and the principles of safety, trustworthiness, choice, collaboration and empowerment alongside respect for diversity, as outlined in [Fallot and Harris's Creating Cultures of Trauma-Informed Care (CCTIC): A Self-Assessment and Planning Protocol (PDF 201KB)](https://children.wi.gov/Documents/CCTICSelf-AssessmentandPlanningProtocol0709.pdf).

body.h2: 9. Glossary
body.h3: Women who have survived domestic abuse
body.text: “Survivors of domestic abuse” refers to the women aged 18 years and over who took part in this research, with current or previous (within the last five years) experiences of living in various types of accommodation because of domestic abuse that are provided through local authorities or services, such as specialist domestic abuse charities, in England. Civil society organisations and service provider gatekeepers assisted this research by identifying survivors of domestic abuse with relevant experience.

body.h2: 10. Methodology
body.text: 10. Methodology

body.h2: 10. Methodology
body.text: From January to March 2023, Interventions Alliance conducted 40 in-depth interviews with women who have survived domestic abuse across England on behalf of the Office for National Statistics (ONS). Interventions Alliance are a specialist provider of justice and social care, with a dedicated in-house research team with previous experience researching domestic abuse.

body.h2: 10. Methodology
body.h3: Approach to sampling and recruitment
body.text: Approach to sampling and recruitment

body.h2: 10. Methodology
body.h3: Approach to sampling and recruitment
body.text: A maximum variation purposive sampling approach was used to gather a wide range of perspectives relating to accommodation experiences. For our definition of accommodation, see [Section 9: Glossary](#9-glossary). The sampling frame for this research focused on achieving a diverse sample of women who have survived domestic abuse and who either had current, or previous accommodation experience, or both, after leaving domestic abuse within the last five years and:

body.h2: 10. Methodology
body.h3: Approach to sampling and recruitment
body.text: had lived in different types of accommodation

body.h2: 10. Methodology
body.h3: Approach to sampling and recruitment
body.text: currently lived in different areas of England (including rural and urban areas)

body.h2: 10. Methodology
body.h3: Approach to sampling and recruitment
body.text: were of different ages and ethnic backgrounds

body.h2: 10. Methodology
body.h3: Approach to sampling and recruitment
body.text: We used this approach to explore how these different characteristics may shape access and engagement experiences. The sample information in our [accompanying dataset](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/crimeandjustice/datasets/womenwhohavesurviveddomesticabuseandtheirexperiencesoftemporarysafeaccommodationsampleinformation) provides aggregate information on the characteristics of participants for the planned and achieved sample. Most survivors had accommodation experiences within the last five years, with the exception of one participant.

body.h2: 10. Methodology
body.h3: Approach to sampling and recruitment
body.text: Participants were recruited through referrals from civil society organisations and are referred to as either “current experience” or “previous experience” based on their situation at the time of their interview.

body.h2: 10. Methodology
body.h3: Design and materials
body.text: Design and materials

body.h2: 10. Methodology
body.h3: Design and materials
body.text: The design of the research and the research materials were developed using trauma-informed practices (see [Section 9: Glossary](#9-glossary)). These practices seek to:

body.h2: 10. Methodology
body.h3: Design and materials
body.text: prevent traumatisation or re-traumatisation

body.h2: 10. Methodology
body.h3: Design and materials
body.text: contribute to and support recovery from trauma

body.h2: 10. Methodology
body.h3: Design and materials
body.text: enable physical and psychological safety for those affected by trauma and for those working with them

body.h2: 10. Methodology
body.h3: Design and materials
body.text: The research also received approval from the National Statistician's Data Ethics Advisory Committee (NSDEC).

body.h2: 10. Methodology
body.h3: Design and materials
body.text: A 10 to 15-minute pre-interview briefing call was held with participants prior to the main interview. This was to outline the research process in detail, ensure informed consent, and provide an opportunity for the participant to ask any questions.

body.h2: 10. Methodology
body.h3: Design and materials
body.text: A participant-led approach was taken in the interviews, which lasted approximately 75 minutes, to allow participants to discuss their journeys and what was most important to them. The flexible, trauma-informed interview format accommodated the specific needs and preferences of each participant, such as checking in with participants during the interview and taking breaks whenever needed. Participant preference for interview mode was discussed during the pre-briefing call, with most interviews conducted online using Microsoft Teams (38), and the remainder in person (2).

body.h2: 10. Methodology
body.h3: Design and materials
body.text: A translation service was offered for those who preferred to participate in a language other than English. Where participant interviews were conducted in a language other than English, translated quotes used in this report have been attributed accordingly.

body.h2: 10. Methodology
body.h3: Design and materials
body.text: Two expert advisory groups guided the research to ensure that all research materials reflected the diverse experiences of survivors. The "experts by profession" advisory group included academics, policy colleagues, domestic abuse charities and regional stakeholder networks. The "experts by experience" advisory group included women who had survived domestic abuse and had experiences of living in different types of accommodation after leaving domestic abuse.

body.h2: 10. Methodology
body.h3: Design and materials
body.text: The participant materials used in the in-depth interviews are available on request from [equalities@ons.gov.uk](mailto:equalities@ons.gov.uk).

body.h2: 10. Methodology
body.h3: Approach to analysis
body.text: Approach to analysis

body.h2: 10. Methodology
body.h3: Approach to analysis
body.text: In-depth interviews were audio recorded following participants' consent and then transcribed verbatim. Interview transcripts were analysed thematically using coding to identify themes, patterns and concepts within participants' accounts.

body.h2: 10. Methodology
body.h3: Approach to analysis
body.text: Initial interview transcripts were coded using open, descriptive coding, with codes subsequently organised into a coding framework. This formed the basis of continued analysis in NVivo 12 (QSR, Australia), with codes being further developed and adapted as analysis progressed.

body.h2: 10. Methodology
body.h3: Approach to analysis
body.text: Findings were constantly compared within and between cases to test and explore initial themes, and differences were actively sought.

body.h2: 10. Methodology
body.h3: Strengths and limitations
body.text: Strengths and limitations

body.h2: 10. Methodology
body.h3: Strengths and limitations
body.text: Strengths of the research include:

body.h2: 10. Methodology
body.h3: Strengths and limitations
body.text: a flexible, participant-led approach to interviews, which enabled a nuanced understanding of how survivors experienced their accommodation journeys, what was important to make them to feel safe, and what could help improve accommodation experiences for survivors in future

body.h2: 10. Methodology
body.h3: Strengths and limitations
body.text: the familiarity and rapport built during a pre-briefing call used to introduce the participant to the research and the researcher, providing an opportunity for questions prior to the interview, and to gain an understanding of participant needs for the interview

body.h2: 10. Methodology
body.h3: Strengths and limitations
body.text: the purposive sampling strategy which achieved a spread of participant characteristics; this encouraged a wide range of participant experiences and accounts to emerge

body.h2: 10. Methodology
body.h3: Strengths and limitations
body.text: participant recruitment through civil society organisations, which meant that survivors already connected with services could access relevant support following the interview if needed, as well as facilitating trust and encouraging participation by working with trusted sources

body.h2: 10. Methodology
body.h3: Strengths and limitations
body.text: support from advisory groups throughout the research process, which ensured the appropriateness and relevance of the research and the research materials, maximising the potential benefit and minimising risk of harm

body.h2: 10. Methodology
body.h3: Strengths and limitations
body.text: Limitations of the research include:

body.h2: 10. Methodology
body.h3: Strengths and limitations
body.text: the generalisability of the research findings, because these are limited to the concepts presented by participants; findings may not apply in different contexts or settings, and may change over time

body.h2: 10. Methodology
body.h3: Strengths and limitations
body.text: the recruitment being heavily reliant on civil society organisation gatekeepers to identify and invite eligible participants; this may have unintentionally excluded potential participants from taking part

body.h2: 10. Methodology
body.h3: Strengths and limitations
body.text: the variation of language used by participants and within policy documents when referring to types of accommodation and services, making it difficult to compare or contrast experiences directly

body.h2: 10. Methodology
body.h3: Strengths and limitations
body.text: the ability to collect details about accommodation and service providers; this was limited because participant recruitment was carried out by a third party

body.h2: 10. Methodology
body.h3: Strengths and limitations
body.text: the ability to capture experiences and barriers which contribute to some survivors not accessing accommodation support, because all participants in this research had accessed accommodation after leaving domestic abuse
